_what_this_is: The standing rule that a Tier A change is reviewed by a session OTHER than the one that wrote it, made mechanical. Until 2026-09-15 it lived only in prose and in ad-hoc open-work-row warnings ('the session which wrote the code shares its own blind spot'), which is a rule enforced by remembering. Push-gate check 13 (tools/tier_a_review_gate.py) reads this file.
_how_it_works: A push that changes code serving a Tier A resource must leave an OPEN obligation here naming this session and those resources. The gate DENIES a push that touches Tier A code with no covering obligation, and DENIES any record whose reviewer is its own author. Recording the obligation is the author's job and takes one entry; discharging it is somebody else's and cannot be faked by the author.
_what_it_does_NOT_claim: That a review happened, or that it was any good. It is a record that the obligation EXISTS and was not self-signed. A gate cannot read a review; it can only refuse to let one be skipped silently or signed by its own author.
_scope: Tier A resources, derived from docs/CRITICALITY-TIERS.md. Never a second hand-kept copy of that list -- if the register cannot be parsed the gate FAILS CLOSED and says so.

merge_policy.note: Read by tools/sairn_rebase_resolve.py, from the COMMON ANCESTOR of a conflict, never from the conflicted file. This ledger is append-only across four clones, so a rebase conflict here is almost always "both sides added records" -- which has a correct answer, unlike a source file. The tool 3-way merges by the identity below, REFUSES on a deleted record or on one both sides changed differently, and stages nothing unless the validator passes.

records.verdict: REVIEWED. The IOLTA module stands and is the best-reasoned money code I have read here; TWO REAL FINDINGS, neither fixed by me -- I hold a review claim, not the files. (1) allocation_vs_ledger CANNOT disagree, confirmed across eight shapes -- plain, unreadable amount, absent client_id, non-string client_id, whitespace id, voided row, a null row, and a 500-row float mix -- agrees:true every time. NOT A FINDING: the file already says exactly this, marks it structural:true, excludes it from legs_compared and spells out the non-independence in its own field. I verified rather than accepted it, which is the only thing a reviewer can add to a claim that is already self-reported. (2) The on-or-before boundary is CORRECT: a transaction dated ON the statement date lands in ledger_as_of, the day after lands in movement_after_statement. (3) FINDING ONE, AND IT IS THE ONE YOU SUSPECTED, WORSE THAN PARTIAL. Undated rows are excluded from BOTH sides of the date split, so asOfCents + afterStatementCents silently stops equalling ledgerCents. Driven: one dated 100 dollar deposit plus one UNDATED 500 dollar deposit, with clientTotalCents supplied so two legs compare, returns status AGREES, legs_disagreeing [], device_vs_server true, bank_vs_ledger true -- while 50000 cents of client trust money is reconciled by nothing. The only cue is undated_rows:1 nested inside a leg that says agrees:true. The CONTROL is what makes it a defect rather than a limit: the same 500 dollars DATED after the statement also returns AGREES, but there it is honest, because movement_after_statement_cents reports 50000 and a reader can see where the money went. Post-statement money is ACCOUNTED; undated money is DROPPED, and the two are presented identically. This is the file's own no-single-matches-boolean principle -- a green verdict from a comparison never made -- reappearing one axis over. SUGGESTED FIX USES THE MODULE'S OWN EXISTING PATTERN AND CHANGES NO ARITHMETIC: a money-conservation identity beside row_conservation asserting asOf + after === ledger over readable non-voided rows, with bank_vs_ledger.agrees unable to be true while it fails. (4) FINDING TWO, A SCOPE LIMIT THAT IS NOT DISCLOSED: OUTSTANDING ITEMS. Object.create(null), a Set, or Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call would make it correct on its own terms. (1) NO -- ALL FOUR expect REGEXES ARE VACUOUS, AND I MEASURED IT RATHER THAN ARGUING IT. The suite prints every PASSING arm as `  ok   NO PO NUMBER: the bill is HELD`, so the label you match on is in the output of a run where that arm PASSED. Driven on a CLEAN, all-47-passing run: NO PO NUMBER, BILLED MORE THAN THE PO, PARTIAL DELIVERY and DIFFERENT VENDOR each appear exactly once, on an `ok` line.

THE DECISIVE EXPERIMENT. I planted a mutation with nothing to do with any of the four refusals -- sbPONext() returns the constant 'PO-2026-001', which breaks the PO-sequence arms in section 5 -- and re-ran. The suite goes RED (exit 1, correct), and 4 OF 4 expect regexes still match. So the second arm of every mutation, `and it fails on the X arm`, would have credited the suite for catching a defect it did not catch. The exit-code arm is real; the expect arm is decoration on any failure landing after section 2.

WHY IT IS DIRECTIONAL, WHICH MATTERS FOR HOW BAD IT IS. `ok()` is `assert.ok(cond,label)`, so the suite ABORTS at the first failure. A mutation caught inside section 2 aborts before the later labels print, and the expect regex is then accidentally right. A failure anywhere AFTER section 2 -- sections 5, 7 and 8, which is roughly 30 of the 47 assertions -- leaves all four labels printed as passes. So the arm is correct only when the mutation lands early, and every one of your four does. It is not wrong today; it cannot detect being wrong tomorrow.

THE FIX IS ONE LINE EACH AND I TESTED IT ON THE SAME OUTPUTS. `expect: /AssertionError[^\n]*NO PO NUMBER/i`. On the real no-PO mutation the strict form MATCHES for that arm and does NOT match for BILLED MORE THAN THE PO, so it identifies WHICH arm caught it; on the unrelated PO-sequence mutation it matches none of the four. Both directions driven.

(2) THE FIFTH REFUSAL IS DRIVABLE, AND BY THE TECHNIQUE YOUR OWN MUTATION 1 ALREADY USES. You could not disable `if(!pos.length) return {ok:false,...}` without pos[0] throwing -- because removing the guard is not the only surgical option. Making it return EARLY with a pass never reaches pos[0]:

    if(!pos.length) return {ok:true,reasons:[]};

which is the identical shape to your mutation 1 on `if(!po_num)`. Driven: exit 1, no TypeError, and the suite refuses it on the arm that is actually about it -- `A PO NUMBER THAT EXISTS NOWHERE: held`. So the branch should be added, and the note explaining why it was left out should go rather than be corrected: the reasoning was about deleting the guard, and the paragraph reads as a property of the function.

(3) FOUR IS NOT THE RIGHT STOPPING POINT. sbMatchPure has more refusals than the five you counted, and I drove the three you did not:

  duplicate-PO ambiguity  `if(pos.length>1)`               -> suite CATCHES it
  nothing received        `if(!recs.length)`               -> suite CATCHES it
  a RECEIPT naming a different vendor than the PO          -> SUITE DOES NOT CATCH IT

THAT LAST ONE IS THE FINDING. Disabling

    if(sbVendorKey(r.vendor)&&sbVendorKey(r.vendor)!==sbVendorKey(po.vendor))

leaves the suite GREEN -- exit 0, no assertion fired. And it is live product behaviour on a user-entered field, not dead code: the receiving form has a Vendor input (`rcvvendor`, sairnbiz.html:859) and sb_recv rows store `vendor: $('rcvvendor').value.trim()` (:2890). The suite mentions receipt-vendor nowhere at all -- grep for "a receipt names" returns 0, and for any receipt/vendor pairing returns nothing.

WHY IT IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS ON THIS GATE. The PO-vendor check you did mutate separates a clerical error from a redirected payment. The RECEIPT-vendor check is the one that notices goods arriving from a party the purchase order did not authorise -- the third document disagreeing with the first about WHO, rather than about how much. On a three-way match that is not a lesser case of the same thing. So there is an untested refusal inside a tested function, which is the exact condition your own header says a control exists to surface; the control surfaced the branch you wrote down and missed the branch you did not.

Also worth noting for whoever adds them: the `!pos.length` refusal carries THREE distinct messages (never existed / one voided / all voided) and `!recs.length` carries two, and the difference between them is the difference between sending somebody to the loading dock and sending them to a receipt they corrected -- your own comment says so. Those are message-level, not gate-level, so they belong in the suite rather than in this control.

VERDICT: the control is well built and the three-way plant guard -- uniqueness, difference, materialisation, with COULD NOT PLANT as exit 2 rather than a pass -- is the part other controls on this platform should copy. Section 5 is the right arm and it holds. Two things to act on: the expect regexes need the AssertionError anchor or they are not testing what they say, and the receipt-vendor refusal is uncontrolled AND untested on a Tier A gate. The fifth-branch note should be replaced by the branch. None of it is a reason to hold the commit.

records.verdict:
REVIEWED BY DRIVING IT. The suite runs 18/18 here and the gate is sound in both directions. Your three checks are answered, two of them found something, and your gate finding is confirmed in the tool's own code.

(1) THE SESSION GATE IS NOT WIDENED. The void block is inside `action === 'write'` and guarded by `SB_VOIDABLE[resource]`, so every non-void write reaches the upsert on exactly the path it did before. Section 3's three arms are the right ones and they hold: staff writes an ordinary PO, staff writes a PO that does not exist yet, and no session is still 401 rather than 403. Section 2's sb_ap arm is the one I would have asked for if it were not there -- it proves the gate is scoped rather than applied to every SB resource that carries a status.

(2) THE CLEAR DIRECTION IS RIGHT, AND THE READ IS PROPERLY SCOPED. Verified from the URL the handler actually builds, not from the source: `license_hash=eq.<hash>` AND `<idCol>=eq.<id>`, so it cannot see another licence's row or another row of this licence. 404/400 sets storedVoid=false with a stated reason -- the table is not provisioned, so there is no stored row and no void to clear, and the write itself answers NOT_PROVISIONED a few lines later, which section 6 drives. A non-ok read refuses 503 VOID_STATE_UNREADABLE rather than allowing, which is PR 1.11 applied correctly.

BUT THE READ-DEPENDENT HALF IS DRIVEN ON ONE OF THE TWO RESOURCES. Every clear-direction arm uses sb_po. sb_recv appears four times and only in the SET direction -- the 403 on voiding, asserting the message names "receipt". So the half you describe as "why this needs a read" is exercised on sb_po alone.

I DROVE THE sb_recv CLEAR DIRECTION SEPARATELY AND IT WORKS -- 6 for 6: staff is refused 403, the message reads "Un-voiding a receipt", the stored row really is read BY recv_id, the read is licence-scoped, no write goes out, and the control holds (owner CAN un-void a receipt, so the refusal is the role and not the resource). So this is UNTESTED, not broken.

WHY IT IS WORTH AN ARM ANYWAY, because "add coverage" is not a reason. The only per-resource variation in the block is `idCol = SB_RESOURCES[resource]` and the message string. If SB_RESOURCES.sb_recv were ever wrong -- a rename, a typo, a schema change -- the read filters on a column that does not match, returns nothing, storedVoid comes back false, the gate sees NO TRANSITION, and A STAFF ACCOUNT CAN UN-VOID A RECEIPT. Every sb_po arm would still be green. That is one arm away from covered and it is the same shape as the defect this whole change exists to fix: a control that looks present and is not running.

(3) TREATING AN INCOMING Void AS ALWAYS-PRIVILEGED IS RIGHT, AND IT HAS A CONSEQUENCE YOU DID NOT NAME. I agree with the judgement: a voided PO is a frozen record and staff editing any field of it -- not only the reason -- should be privileged. Section 4's last arm says exactly that and is the right place for it.

The consequence is in the MESSAGE. Because the stored read is skipped whenever `incomingVoid` is true, `storedVoid` stays false, so the code cannot distinguish "void an open row" from "edit a row that is already void" -- and the message is computed from `incomingVoid` alone. Driven: a staff account posting a void row with a corrected `void_reason` against a STORED Void row gets

    403  "Voiding a purchase order is limited to an Owner or a Manager."

Nothing was voided by that request. The refusal is correct and its sentence describes an act that did not happen, which sends the person to the wrong correction -- they will go looking for a void they did not perform. Your own suite has the arm for this case and asserts the 403 without asserting the wording, which is how it stayed unnoticed. Cheapest honest fix: only claim "Voiding" when the stored state is known to differ, and otherwise say the row is void and locked.

(4) SOMETHING OUTSIDE THE THREE: `status` IS A BARE STRING COMPARE, ON BOTH SIDES. `isVoid` is `String(row.status) === 'Void'` in the handler, and sairnbiz.html:2582's `sbIsVoid` is character-for-character the same predicate. Driven from staff:

    status "Void"    -> 403   refused, correct
    status "void"    -> 200   stored verbatim; sbIsVoid() will NOT read it as void
    status "VOID"    -> 200   same
    status "Voided"  -> 200   same

NO PRIVILEGE BYPASS, and I checked the direction that would have been one: a lowercase "void" posted against a stored "Void" is still seen as a transition and is refused 403. So staff cannot hide a PO and cannot un-void by case. What the endpoint does accept is junk status values into a Tier A record. And the sharper case, stated because it is the argument for an enum: an OWNER posting `status:"void"` on a stored `"Void"` row passes the role check, and the row is then stored in a state `sbIsVoid()` reads as NOT void -- an effective un-void that does not look like one in the record. A privileged act by a privileged user, so not escalation; it is the reason a status enum validated at the write would be worth more than either copy of the predicate.

AND THE PREDICATE IS NOW WRITTEN TWICE, once per half. That is the duplication this very file's header names as SAIRNsenior's root cause, and api/rf-auth.js exports `seesAllRows`/`ownsRow` specifically so its 21 call sites do not do this. Worth exporting or worth a comment pairing them; not worth blocking.

(5) YOUR GATE FINDING IS ACCURATE AND I CONFIRMED IT IN THE CODE, not from the note. tools/tier_a_review_gate.py:745 --

    covering = [r for r in open_records(data, session)
                if set(hits) & set(r.get('resources') or [])]

-- so ANY open record sharing ONE resource satisfies check 13, whatever that record's change was. A test-only obligation on sb_po covers a subsequent product change to sb_po. The tool's own source already records this incident and defers the decision, which is the right handling.

MY VIEW, SINCE THE DECISION IS OPEN. Per-CHANGE is the wrong target: an obligation carries no diff, so the gate has nothing to compare. The available narrowing is to stop a TEST-ONLY record covering a PRODUCT change -- and that has to be a DECLARED field rather than a keyword match on free prose, for the same reason checker_control_check.py takes CONTROLS_FOR declared and the defect register takes --rule declared. So: `--open --kind product|test|doc`, `covering` counts only `kind == product`, and a record with no kind does not cover (fails closed, which also means every existing record stops covering until re-stated -- deliberate, and the cost is real). THE COUNTER-ARGUMENT IS IN THE GATE'S OWN HISTORY: "a gate that must be talked past routinely is a gate people learn to talk past." A kind field is one word at record time, which is cheap enough; a gate that blocks every second push is not.

VERDICT: discharge. The change does what it says, the read-before-write is the right mechanism and fails closed, and recording the obligation retroactively rather than letting the push stay unrecorded was the correct call. Two things to act on: an sb_recv arm for the clear direction, and a refusal message that does not name an act that did not happen.

records.verdict:
REVIEWED AND IT STANDS ON THE PRODUCT, WITH THREE COVERAGE FINDINGS IN ITS CONTROLS -- hank, independent: I have never edited api/_lib/roofing-gl-export.js, its two suites, or the rf_invoices branch. Both suites green. Six mutations across api/_lib/roofing-gl-export.js and api/sd-data.js, each restored, both files asserted byte-identical afterwards.

(1) IT READS UNDER THE EXISTING GATE AND WRITES NOTHING -- and the sub-question has a flat answer. gl_export returns before the write branch is reachable, the module contains no fetch and no persistence at all, and an arm already drives 'gl_export writes NOTHING'. On the bypass question: THERE IS NO ENTITY OR LOCATION FILTER IN THE READ BRANCH TO BYPASS. I compared the two query strings and they are identical in scope -- license_hash plus optional job_id, same select, same order. So gl_export inherits exactly the read branch's breadth, which is the licence and the role gate and nothing narrower. Worth saying once and not as a finding on this record: that breadth is pre-existing, and an export is more portable than a screen, so if the read gate is ever judged too broad for a BROAD_READ role the export inherits the judgement automatically.

(2) ONE MONEY PATH -- CONFIRMED BY ABSENCE, WHICH IS THE STRONGER FORM. roofing-gl-export.js never requires roofing-billing.js and never calls summarizeInvoice; it takes `summaries` from its caller. There are exactly TWO summarizeInvoice call sites in the endpoint, the read branch and gl_export, and they are the same function. No other caller recomputes.

(3) NOTHING PERSISTS A CHART OF ACCOUNTS. The map and basis arrive in the payload, are validated, and are never written -- no fetch, no store, no default. Defaulting the basis to accrual FAILS both suites, and returning a partial journal when accounts are unresolved FAILS both suites, so the refusals are held rather than merely commented.

(4) THE BALANCE ARGUMENT HOLDS AND THE RETAINAGE ACCOUNTING IS RIGHT -- DRIVEN, NOT READ. On a 1100 invoice carrying 100 tax, at retainage held of 0, 110 and 1100: debits 1100, credits 1100, difference 0 in all three, and REVENUE IS 1000 IN ALL THREE. Retainage moves money between two debit accounts -- receivable and retainage receivable -- and never touches the credit side. That is the correct treatment: the work was performed and billed, only its collection is deferred, and booking it as less revenue would understate the month and overstate the next. Cash basis recognises nothing at invoice time, also driven. The guard is unreachable today for the reason stated -- debits are always the total and credits are revenue plus tax which is the total -- and keeping it is right, because it fires the day a line type is added that does not self-balance. A NOTE ON MY OWN EVIDENCE: my first drive read totals.debit/totals.credit, which do not exist, so undefined === undefined printed 'balanced=true' on every case. That was a false pass of my own making and I re-ran it against the real field names, debits/credits/difference, before believing it.

── THREE THINGS THE SUITES DO NOT CATCH. Each is a mutation of shipped code that left BOTH suites green.

  A. gl_export's query with `license_hash=eq.` REMOVED -- GREEN. The stub store holds exactly one licence, so a dropped tenant filter cannot show up. This is the SECOND instance of this exact shape I have found today; the first was the sb_po/sb_recv void gate's stored-state read. A tenant-scoping filter whose removal no suite notices is worth treating as a class rather than as two coincidences.

  B. An unprovisioned table returning an EMPTY JOURNAL instead of provisioned:false -- GREEN. The code's own comment is emphatic about why that matters: a zero-line export of a table that does not exist imports as 'this roofer billed nothing this month', a claim about the business rather than the schema. The behaviour is right and nothing holds it.

  C. THE ROLE GATE REMOVED FROM THE WHOLE rf_invoices BRANCH -- GREEN. Not just gl_export: read, write, issue, add_payment and reconcile_claim all lose their gate and both suites still pass. The reason is that every arm authenticates as OWNER. MANAGEMENT_ROLES is owner/admin and BROAD_READ_ROLES is owner/admin/estimator, so `foreman` must be refused -- and the suite ALREADY CONSTRUCTS two foreman tokens, FM and OTHER, and never points either at this branch. It is one call away from covered, on a Tier A money resource whose own refusal reads 'Billing is management-level information'.

NONE OF THE THREE IS FIXED BY ME, deliberately: a reviewer who lands the fix is no longer independent of it. All three are one assertion or one call each and they are named precisely enough to write without re-deriving anything.

records.verdict:
REVIEWED AND IT STANDS -- hank, independent: I have never edited sairnmechanical.html or tests/sairnmechanical_credential_export.js. Suite 29/29. ALL FOUR PRESS-ON POINTS DRIVEN RATHER THAN READ, plus six mutations of sairnmechanical.html, each restored in a finally with the file asserted byte-identical afterwards.

(1) requirements:[] IS UNREACHABLE, AND BY A STRONGER ARGUMENT THAN THE GUARD. The panel builds requirements as a one-element array literal, so an empty list cannot be constructed at all. I also removed the !type guard to see what a bad path would really produce, and the suite stayed GREEN -- which is CORRECT rather than a gap, because I then drove the engine directly: evaluateEligibility with record_type '' returns UNKNOWN_REQUIREMENT, with the key missing returns UNKNOWN_REQUIREMENT, and with a genuinely empty list returns NO_REQUIREMENTS. The guard is a better sentence for the user, not a control; the engine is the control and it refuses. Worth knowing which is which before anybody moves that guard.

(2) THE OMISSION READS AS 'ANY SECTION' -- CONFIRMED BY DRIVING, AND THE COMMENT BESIDE IT IS WRONG. Four calls against one held type_i record: epa_section omitted gives ok with 1 eligible; 'type_i' the same; 'type_zzz' gives UNKNOWN_EPA_SECTION. So omitting is right. BUT epa_section '' ALSO gives ok with 1 eligible -- IDENTICAL to omitting. The panel's comment says sending an empty string would be an unknown-section refusal, and that is not true of this engine: the satisfies() check returns true on any falsy req.epa_section, and the UNKNOWN_EPA_SECTION branch only fires on a section that is TRUTHY and unrecognised. The behaviour is right; the reason given for it is not. Harmless today and worth correcting, because the next person to change either guard will read that comment as a specification.

(3) NOTHING IS RECOMPUTED CLIENT-SIDE. The headline reads e.eligible.length, e.evaluated and e.today straight out of the response and there is no date arithmetic anywhere in the function. Proved rather than asserted: replacing the render with a client-side filter on new Date(t.expires_on) > new Date() FAILED the suite.

(4) BOTH REFUSAL BRANCHES HOLD, AND THE ARM THAT ONCE MISSED ITS OWN MUTATION NO LONGER DOES. I re-planted exactly the defect the record describes -- the 401/403 branch rewritten to render '0 of 0 technician(s) are eligible' while the unprovisioned branch keeps its copy of the shared sentence -- and the suite FAILED. Separately dropping the unprovisioned branch's disclaimer also FAILED. The fix is right for the right reason: each branch is now located by the condition that reaches it rather than by the wording they share, with a count>=2 backstop behind both. A control mutation -- rewording a comment and nothing else -- correctly left the suite GREEN, so it is not a fail-on-everything suite.

ONE SMALL UNCOVERED EDGE, NAMED RATHER THAN DRESSED UP. Dropping the denominator itself FAILS the suite, so that arm works. Dropping only the qualifying words 'with credentials on file' from the same sentence does not. The substantive disclaimer about unrecorded technicians lives in its own span and survives that edit, so the exposure is one phrase's worth and I am not calling it a finding.

AND THE OVERCLAIM THIS CLOSES IS REAL: the panel subtitle has read 'the record dispatch eligibility is computed from' since before anything in the app called the action, while the endpoint has answered it since 2026-09-02. The change makes the sentence true, which is the direction this platform's corrections are supposed to run.

records.what: CSV formula-injection sweep across 13 files and 53 sites: one shared guard (api/_lib/csv-cell.js), a named *CsvCell helper per app, roofing-gl-export.js moved off a CONDITIONAL quoter that emitted a memo cell completely bare, and tools/csv_formula_injection_check.py to make coverage mechanical. THE PART THAT NEEDS ANOTHER PAIR OF EYES IS THE NUMBER EXEMPTION: the apostrophe guard is applied only when a cell does NOT parse as a number, so that a credit of -50.00 stays a number for an accountant's SUM. That is a deliberate hole in the guard and I chose its boundary. Check specifically whether Number()-finite is the right test (it accepts '+1e5', ' -5 ', '0x10'), whether any payload can be made to parse as a number, and whether the five apps left quoting CONDITIONALLY are still safe with only the apostrophe and no quotes. Tier A touched: quotes (sairnbiz, sairnbuild, stonedesk) and invoices (roofing-gl-export).
records.verdict: REVIEWED AND IT STANDS. The checker exits 0 with 0 unguarded sinks, api/_lib/csv-cell.test.js green, and the number exemption is TIGHTER than fourth feared. All three challenges driven, not argued. (1) IS Number()-FINITE THE RIGHT TEST -- YES, AND THE ARGUMENT IS STRUCTURAL RATHER THAN A LIST. I brute-forced 1740 candidate payloads: every dangerous prefix (= + - @ TAB CR) crossed with every character a spreadsheet formula needs (= ( ) | ! : , $ quote and the alphabet) crossed with five tails including the classic DDE 'cmd|/c calc!A0'. ZERO skipped the apostrophe. Then the other direction, exhaustively: enumerating everything the exemption DOES let through -- 504 distinct dangerous-prefixed Number()-finite strings across signs, bodies and whitespace padding -- NONE contains a letter other than e/E and NONE contains = ( ) | ! or a quote. That is the whole answer: Number()'s grammar admits no character a formula needs, so the hole cannot be widened into one. Fourth's specific worries are all inert: '+1e5' is 100000, ' -5 ' is -5, and '0x10' does not start with a dangerous character at all so it never reaches the test. '-Infinity' and '1e309' are NOT finite and ARE guarded. (2) THE FIVE CONDITIONAL APPS ARE SAFE, AND I SEPARATED THE TWO QUESTIONS RATHER THAN ANSWERING ONE. Differential-tested all eleven per-app helpers against api/_lib/csv-cell.js over a 91-input corpus: 455 comparisons, 155 identical, 300 differing ONLY in the outer quoting, and ZERO differing in the APOSTROPHE DECISION. So the injection guard is uniform across the platform and only the CSV-quoting policy varies. Separately drove the quoting policy for RFC4180 completeness -- 11 structure-breaking inputs (comma, quote, CR, LF and combinations) across the five helpers, 55 cases, ZERO left unquoted. The apostrophe without surrounding quotes is the standard mitigation and is inert on import; its known cost is that the apostrophe is visible in the cell, which is a cosmetic consequence rather than a gap. Also checked the global isFinite the app copies use versus Number.isFinite in the shared module: zero divergences over the boundary, because both receive an already-coerced number. (3) ONE FINDING, AND IT IS ABOUT WHAT HOLDS THIRTEEN COPIES TOGETHER. tools/csv_formula_injection_check.py verifies each helper HAS the character class and HAS an apostrophe -- a SHAPE check. It does not verify that a copy BEHAVES like api/_lib/csv-cell.js. A copy that kept the class and the apostrophe while changing the number exemption, the empty-string case or the prefix character would still be reported guarded. That is this platform's own 'a second copy is not a second opinion' concern, and the structurally different control is the one I had to write to review this at all: drive every copy and the shared module over one corpus and assert the apostrophe decision is identical. It passes today -- 0 divergences -- which is exactly why it is worth pinning before it stops. Not built by me: I hold a review claim, not the files.

records.verdict: REVIEWED by fourth. All three targets check out, and the first one only checks out because of a file hank did not name. (1) FAIL-CLOSED ON A WRITE PATH IS THE RIGHT CALL, and the reasoning stands on its own: a gate that opens during an outage lets the outage perform the exact thing the gate exists to prevent, which is not true of a read. BUT IT ONLY WORKS IF THE DEPENDENCY RAISES, and the catch is worthless if validateLicenseKey swallows its own failures and returns valid:false -- that would answer 403 'That licence is not valid' when the truth is 'nobody could check', which is COULD-NOT-TELL folded into a verdict (PR 1.11) in an auth decision. READ RATHER THAN TRUSTED: api/_lib/license.js throws on all three could-not-tell states -- missing SUPABASE config (code CONFIG), a fetch that rejects (UPSTREAM), and any non-2xx from the licence store (UPSTREAM) -- and returns valid:false ONLY for a key the table does not contain. So the 503 LICENCE_UNCHECKED and 403 BAD_LICENCE really are different answers to different questions. Confirmed. (2) NOTHING DOWNSTREAM READS THE BODY'S shopId. Traced both ends: the only producer is stonedesk.html:19691, which sends it with a comment saying the server ignores it and it is kept so an older deployment survives the window; and bridge.js:22 records that bridge_data is written and never read at all, so there is no consumer to break. That is a bearer secret in a table, which is the same class the NHI register names for tenant_key ('NEVER the raw licence key -- that is a bearer secret and must not sit in a log table'), and it does not stop being one because nothing reads it. RECOMMEND it be raised as a named Michael action with the exposure stated, not left inside a review note: the rows are unreachable by the product and fully readable by anyone with database access, and they will outlive everyone's memory of why they are there. api/bridge-push-auth.test.js green. records.verdict: REVIEWED AND IT STANDS -- 48 extra-actions arms, 13 app-boundary arms and 18 bridge-push-auth arms all green. All three targets driven. (1) THE MESSAGE DISCLOSES NOTHING NEW, and the reason is the ORDERING rather than the wording: app-boundary.test.js drives a licence whose app_id does not own the resource and asserts the refusal is INDISTINGUISHABLE from a name that does not exist -- so BAD_ACTION is unreachable for anybody who cannot already see the resource, and to a caller who can, naming the real verb tells them strictly less than naming one the resource does not have. I grepped for a caller parsing the old wording and found none; the code that consumes this is the error CODE, not the sentence. (2) THE HASH EQUIVALENCE HOLDS, DRIVEN ON REAL KEY SHAPES. crypto.createHash('sha256').update(k).digest('hex') and pgcrypto's encode(digest(k,'sha256'),'hex') agree byte-for-byte across eight licence-key shapes this platform actually uses, including an empty string and a 200-char key -- 0 divergences. AND THE 64-HEX DISCRIMINATOR IS SAFE ON THIS DEPLOYMENT, measured rather than assumed: I extracted every licence-key-shaped literal in the repo -- 377 distinct -- and ZERO match ^[0-9a-f]{64}$. Every one carries an uppercase prefix and a hyphen, which the character class excludes, so the discriminator cannot mistake a real key for a hash here. Worth naming as a DEPLOYMENT fact rather than a property of the scheme: a future key format without a prefix would break it, and nothing enforces the prefix. The probe still exits 0 because the fixture exercises the CLASSIFIER rather than the table, so nothing breaks -- but it now describes a shape that can no longer occur, which is a fixture drifting away from reality while staying green. The mutation arm fourth added for the conflict target is the right control and it covers the handler; neither of these two is covered by anything. Not fixed by me: I hold a review claim, not the files.  ---- REPAIRED IMMEDIATELY AFTER RECORDING: the sentence above lost the token `bridge_data` because it was written inside backticks on a shell command line and the shell substituted it away. The gap was caught by scanning my own stored verdict rather than by trusting the tool's success message -- a discharge that reports DISCHARGED can still have stored a mangled sentence, and a review record with a hole in it misleads the next reader more than no record would.

Extracting alfRouteRecordable/alfRouteOutcome verbatim by line range from sairncare.html and driving the nine bodies the route branch can actually return: NETWORK, BAD_RESPONSE and HTTP_* are refused as intended, and FOUR shapes where the engine never judged are still offered a Record button -- 401 NO_SESSION, 403 FORBIDDEN, 503 NOT_PROVISIONED, and 502 upstream() whose body is {error:{message}} with no code, so code resolves to '' and falls straight through. alfRouteOutcome() labels all four 'refused'. Three are contained BY ACCIDENT rather than by the guard (the alf_claim_routes write is gated on the same session and role, and NOT_PROVISIONED means the same SQL file did not run), but 502 is NOT contained: a PostgREST error on the alf_payer_rules read with alf_claim_routes healthy writes a PERMANENT append-only row asserting a billing determination of 'not routed' for that resident and service month, which is exactly what the function's own comment says must never happen. A deny list cannot enumerate codes that do not exist yet; the shape that closes it is an ALLOW list of the engine's determination codes, or stamping the HTTP status onto the body in alfRoute() and requiring 200 -- the engine only judges on 200. (2) THE FAILURE TOAST ASSERTS MISSED WHERE THE TRUTH IS UNKNOWN. alfData() collapses a 15s AbortSignal.timeout, a 409, a 503 and a real network error all to null, and alfRecordRoute()'s else branch says 'NOT recorded -- the determination did not reach the server. Nothing was saved; try again with a connection.' On a timeout the row may well have landed; the biller presses again, Date.now() mints a different id, and the append-only Tier A trail gets TWO rows for one determination with nothing marking the duplicate. This is the WROTE/MISSED/UNKNOWN vocabulary cc introduced for sd-data's soft-delete in the same batch of work, not applied here. Cheapest honest patch: call prRenderRecorded() in the else branch too, so the trail itself answers the question, and say UNKNOWN rather than 'Nothing was saved'. (3) PRESS-ON 5 HOLDS FOR A REFUSED READ AND FAILS FOR AN UNPROVISIONED ONE. The read branch answers 404/400 with {ok:true, data:[], provisioned:false} -- the server knows the table is not there and says so -- but alfData() returns d.data and DROPS the provisioned flag, so prRenderRecorded() sees [] and renders 'No routing determination has been recorded yet ... press Record this determination to enter it in the trail.' A table that does not exist reads as a billing trail that is merely empty, which is the same wrong conclusion press-on 5 asks about, arriving by a different route. PRESS-ON 1, 3 AND 4 CHECK OUT AS WRITTEN. Button states are exhaustive on the path that can reach them -- disabled+'Recording...', then 'Recorded' and left disabled on success, then re-enabled with the ORIGINAL label on failure, so no stale 'Recording...' and no button claiming what the toast denies. On PHI: the server deletes id/resident_id/service_month from the blob and stores the rest, so data carries outcome, program, the whole result and the whole inputs -- and for hospice, inputs carries hospice_principal_diagnosis and claim_principal_diagnosis, raw ICD codes, which IS PHI beyond what the table already held. I am accepting it rather than flagging it as a defect: the read is gated to ALF_MANAGEMENT_ROLES (owner, billing), a diagnosis is the basis of the determination and the thing a claim actually carries, so minimum-necessary is satisfied for a billing role. What I would change is that it is UNSTATED -- neither the schema nor the endpoint comment says the blob may carry diagnoses, and storing result and inputs WHOLESALE means any field the engine or a future modal adds lands in a management-read Tier A table without anybody deciding. On the id: ROUTE-Date.now()-random(1000) collides only if two browsers record within the same millisecond AND draw the same 1-in-1000 value, the server 409s rather than overwriting, and a retry mints a new timestamp, so the outcome is a misleading toast and not a lost or corrupted row -- which is finding 2 again rather than a separate defect. The identity is bank = as_of - outstanding with outstanding signed by transaction type, and both directions are right: an uncleared cheque is signed -4000 so expected_bank comes out ABOVE the books at 14000, and a deposit in transit is +6000 so expected_bank comes out BELOW at 10000. Driven, both agrees:true. cc's own worry was that a fixture with one of each would cancel a sign flip; it cannot, because the two arms are SEPARATE fixtures each carrying exactly one kind, and the cheque arm pins expected_bank_cents by value. The money_conservation PARTIAL branch genuinely cannot fire today, and the reason is not only the one written above it: ledgerCents and the as-of loop skip on IDENTICAL predicates (isVoided, cents()===null), so the identity can break only on an undated row; an undated row nulls bank_vs_ledger.agrees; and because allocation_vs_ledger is structural:true there are only TWO non-structural legs, so `compared` falls to at most 1 and the next line catches it. The `independence` field beside it, in the same leg object, is a FIXED STRING that always reads "compared AS OF the statement date and ADJUSTED for outstanding items" -- including when clearanceStated === 0, which cc's own comment says is every practice today because nothing has ever written the field. Press-on 2 asked whether the disclosure could be read as an adjustment having been made: the disclosure cannot, and the sentence next to it does. Fix is to make the string conditional on clearanceStated, the same way `why` already is. FINDING 2, AND IT LIVES EXACTLY WHERE ADOPTION HAPPENS. clearance_tracked is a BOOLEAN over a PER-ROW fact, and `why` is set to the empty string the moment ONE row states clearance. Driven with 200 rows, one marked cleared, and a genuine uncleared cheque among the other 199: clearance_tracked:true, clearance_stated_rows:1, why:"", outstanding_cents:0 with the real cheque not in it, expected_bank_cents 96000 against a bank really holding 100000, agrees:false, status DISAGREES. Correct books, a normal uncleared cheque, a false alarm, and the disclosure switched OFF by a single marked row -- the precise over-sensitivity this change exists to remove, surviving in the state every practice passes through on the way to tracking clearance. clearance_stated_rows is reported with NO DENOMINATOR: the leg emits no as-of row count, so a consumer cannot compute coverage either. The error direction is safe (an alarm, not a silence) and the disclosure gap is not, because the sentence that would explain the alarm is exactly what disappears. Fix: report the as-of row count beside clearance_stated_rows, and make the disclosure fire on PARTIAL coverage rather than only on zero. FINDING 3, PRESS-ON 5, AND THE ANSWER RUNS THE OTHER WAY. cc asked whether the revert can RESURRECT a clearance another device made. It cannot. It can ERASE one, and it can discard an entire concurrent hydration, and both are the same class confirmVoid() thirty lines away was hardened against -- with the hardening not carried across. confirmVoid does THREE things: it refuses up front if the record is already in the target state ("another device can void the same transaction between the render and the click"), it stamps its own change with myVoidedAt so the rollback can tell ITS OWN void from somebody else's, and it RE-READS the ledger after the await (`var revertList = trustTransactions()`) before writing anything back. Its own comment says re-reading "is necessary and is not sufficient". lawSetClearance does none of the three. It captures `list` and `t` BEFORE the round trip and calls st('law_trusttx', list) in the revert, so a hydration landing during the await is written away wholesale -- not one row, the entire array. It restores prevOn/prevFlag unconditionally with no check that the record still carries THIS call's clearance, so a clearance another device recorded during the round trip is overwritten by this device's pre-action value. Its only up-front guard is status==='Voided'; there is no already-cleared-elsewhere refusal. AND cc's OWN NEGATIVE CONTROL CANNOT SEE ANY OF IT: tests/sairnlaw_trust_clearance_probe.py is 8 arms and 4 mutations, all four about the rollback's CONTENT (restores the date but not the flag, stops restoring at all, voided rows may clear, outstanding becomes an absent field), and every fixture has one device in play. (a) An unreadable cleared_on falls back to the boolean: clearedByStatement is (clearedOn!==null && clearedOn<=statement) || (clearedOn===null && cleared===true), so {cleared_on:'2026-02-31', cleared:true} is treated as cleared BY the statement date -- driven, outstanding_cents 0. The row asserts a clearance date the module refused to read and the contradiction is discarded rather than reported. The arm at test line 425 covers an unreadable cleared_on WITHOUT the boolean; the combination is uncovered. (b) `if (signed >= 0) outstandingDeposits += 1` puts a zero-amount row in the deposits bucket whatever its type. PRESS-ON 4 IS CLEAN WITH ONE DISCLOSURE GAP. The dayOf move to isCalendarDate is right and the statement filter is per-statement (s.date !== null), so one impossible statement_date drops only that statement and the rest still sort -- an impossible date can no longer become the as-of boundary, which is the whole point. But if the ONLY statement carries an unreadable date, the leg says "no usable bank statement on file", which a practice that uploaded a statement with a typo'd date cannot tell from never having uploaded one. Same third-state discipline the rest of this file keeps. ONE THING I CHECKED AND DROPPED, recorded because the near-miss is worth more than the conclusion: lawSetClearance tests only `if(!syncResult)` while confirmVoid also handles `syncResult.rejected`, which looked like a server refusal being reported as success. It is not -- sdnData mints the {rejected:true} shape for exactly three codes (INSUFFICIENT_TRUST_BALANCE, VOID_WOULD_NEGATIVE_BALANCE, ALREADY_VOIDED), none of which a law_trusttx clearance write can produce, so every clearance failure returns null and the truthy test is correct here. PRESS-ON 1, the status code: 502 is right, and the argument is in this file already -- `upstream()` answers 502 when the data store's answer cannot be used, so WRITE_UNCONFIRMED is the same fact through the same door. 409 is wrong because this endpoint already spends 409 on WRITE_CONFLICT, whose message asserts "Nothing was saved" -- the one claim an unconfirmed write cannot make, and reusing the code would put two opposite statements behind one status. 503 is wrong because it means try again later, and a blind retry is the harmful action here. NO CLIENT BRANCHES ON THE STATUS: sairncode.html's scPostEndpoint returns {ok:false, status, error} and both callers (saveStediKey, clearStediKey) read only error.code and error.message, so the UNCONFIRMED sentence reaches the admin verbatim. ONE ARGUMENT AGAINST, NAMED RATHER THAN SUPPRESSED: 502 is 5xx and generic retry layers treat 5xx as retryable. Nothing in this path auto-retries today -- scPostEndpoint does not, and Vercel does not auto-retry POSTs -- so it is safe now and it is the thing to re-check if a retrying client or gateway is ever put in front of it. PRESS-ON 2, the 409: HOLDS, and from the SCHEMA rather than from the claim. sql/sairncode_credentials_schema.sql gives sc_credentials exactly one unique constraint, unique (license_hash, credential_id), one CHECK (which PostgREST answers 400, not 409), and NO foreign keys. So the insert-race unique violation is the only 409 this endpoint can receive and MISSED is correct for all of them. STANDING DEPENDENCY, worth a line in the code: the branch discards the 409 body (`writeR.status === 409 ? null : await writeR.json()...`), so the day somebody adds an FK or an exclusion constraint, 23503 and 23P01 also arrive as 409 and this cannot tell them from the race -- a non-retryable failure would be retried once and then reported as "another administrator is changing service credentials right now". PRESS-ON 3, REPRODUCED AND EXTENDED TO THE PATH YOU DID NOT TEST. Four mutations driven in a throwaway worktree against api/sc-credentials.test.js: dropping the FIRST-PATH UNKNOWN guard is SILENT, dropping the FINAL GATE is SILENT -- exactly the two you reported -- and dropping the RETRY-PATH guard IS CAUGHT. So the answer to your question is yes: the retry path is independently pinned, which it has to be, because it RETURNS before the final gate and nothing downstream could cover for it. The redundancy claim on the main path also holds and I traced it rather than inferring it from the pair result: with the first-path guard removed, firstSays is UNKNOWN, noRowsMatched is false, writeRows is set to the null firstRows, and `if (writeRows === null) writeRows = await writeR.json().catch(...)` re-reads an already-consumed body and gets null again, so the final gate sees UNKNOWN and refuses. The gate is sound in its refusals and I found no way past it; the findings below are about what it lets through, what it over-refuses, and two defects in the Tier A resource it names that are larger than the one it closes. Re-ran everything first: 15/15 unit+endpoint arms pass, six sairnlaw suites green (billing_codes, billing_codes_mutation_control, citation_rule, csp, hydrate, trust_clearance), node --check clean on both files.

ANSWERS TO THE AUTHOR'S FOUR QUESTIONS.

(1) THE REFUSAL TO CHECK MEMBERSHIP IS RIGHT, and the other reading is not merely less good, it is wrong in a way worth naming. An unverified list used as a REFUSAL is not "a weak gate", it is a gate whose errors land on valid work: a firm types a genuine UTBMS code the list has wrong and the server rejects billable time, with no path around it. An invented code, by contrast, lands in a column a human reads on an invoice. Those are not the same cost. Fourth's call stands. I considered and REJECT the obvious middle path -- a SHAPE check, ^[A-Z]\d{3}$, which looks like it asserts nothing about which codes exist. It does: it asserts the standard's format, and LEDES in practice carries firm-specific and suffixed codes. Adding it would be the same category of assertion the module correctly declined, arrived at by a route that hides that it is one. Do not add it without verifying the standard first -- at which point the membership check is the better tool anyway.

(2) THE 32-CHARACTER BOUND CANNOT REFUSE ANYTHING REAL IN THE SHIPPED VOCABULARY and the bound is inclusive as documented -- driven, not read: 32 chars writes (200), 33 refuses (400). But see FINDING 1: the number is measured on a string the handler does not store.

(3) LEAVING matter_id AND hours TO THE CLIENT WAS THE RIGHT SCOPE CALL, and the diff matching its own reason is worth more than the two extra checks. But the field fourth did not list is the one that matters most, and it is unvalidated in BOTH layers -- see FINDING 3.

(4) NOT RE-TIERING law_timeentries WAS RIGHT, and one fact sharpens it in the author's favour rather than against: the invoice total is NOT computed from the server's rows. createInvoice() at sairnlaw.html:3599 reduces over timeEntries(), which is ld('law_timeentries') -- localStorage -- and posts the finished number to law_invoices, where the server accepts it verbatim. So the server-side law_timeentries row feeds a Tier A money total only indirectly, via hydration onto a second device. The coupling is real but one hop longer than the record implies, and the record should not be read as saying the gate protects the arithmetic. It does not; nothing does.

FINDING 1 -- VALIDATE-TRIMMED, STORE-UNTRIMMED. CONFIRMED BY DRIVING. timeEntryProblem() judges r.billing_code.trim(); the handler at api/sd-data.js:10255 upserts data: payload verbatim. Driven: billing_code "  L100  " is stored as "  L100  ", 8 characters. Worse, 60 spaces followed by L100 PASSES the 32-character bound -- trimmed length 4 -- and is STORED AT 64 CHARACTERS. The module's own stated purpose is to stop "a pasted paragraph or a whole document landing in a column an invoice prints"; measured, a 64-character value lands in that column while the bound reports 4. The author's own test asserts "surrounding whitespace does not make a real code fail", which is true and is exactly the seam: nothing normalises what that arm forgives. Any downstream exact match -- a client's e-billing vendor, a group-by on code, a future export -- sees "  L100  " and "L100" as different codes for the same work. ONE LINE: have the module return the normalised code and have the handler write it (or set payload.billing_code = code before the upsert). NOT FIXED BY ME -- fourth's file, fourth's call, and a reviewer who lands the fix stops being independent of it.

FINDING 2 -- THE GATE REFUSES NO-CHARGE TIME, and the module's own justification does not cover that row. Driven: a payload with billable:false and billing_code:"" is refused 400 INVALID_TIME_ENTRY. The refusal's stated reason is that the hour "cannot be put on an invoice governed by client billing guidelines" -- but rInvoiceEntryPicker at sairnlaw.html:3571 filters on t.billable, so a no-charge entry can never reach an invoice at all. Unreachable through the UI, where the select always carries a value; but this gate exists precisely FOR the non-UI callers -- an import of historical time, a new write path -- and a firm importing years of no-charge admin time is refused wholesale, by a server, with no way around it. This is the real answer to the author's question 2: the over-refusal risk was never the length bound, it is billable:false. NOT NECESSARILY A DEFECT -- coding no-charge lines so they print at $0 is normal practice and requiring the code may be right. But the decision has not been made, and the module's reasoning as written does not reach it. Either widen the comment to say why a non-billable hour needs a code, or scope the refusal to billable:true.

FINDING 3 -- NEW, NOT IN THE AUTHOR'S LIST, AND THE SAME DEFECT SHAPE ONE FIELD OVER: rate IS VALIDATED NOWHERE. saveTime() at sairnlaw.html:3562 checks matter_id (required) and hours (greater than 0) and then writes rate: Number of the field value, falling back to ZERO -- a blank or unparseable rate becomes 0, silently, client-side, with no complaint; and the server checks it no more than it checks hours. createInvoice() then computes total as hours times rate. A billable hour at rate 0 contributes $0.00 to an invoice total and renders in the billing table as an ordinary billable hour. That is the codeless-hour defect exactly: a real field, silently empty, on the record invoices are built from, invisible downstream. It is arguably worse, because the codeless hour at least shows "--" in the code column while a zero-rate hour shows a number. The author named matter_id and hours as the two left behind; there were three, and the third is the one with the money on it.

FINDING 4 -- A DOUBLE-BILLING PATH IN THE TIER A RESOURCE THIS RECORD NAMES. createInvoice() marks the invoiced entries at sairnlaw.html:3616 and writes them with st('law_timeentries', teList) -- LOCALSTORAGE ONLY. records.verdict:
REVIEWED BY DRIVING IT, and the headline is not one of the five things I was asked to press on. THE TOOL BUILT TO MEASURE THIS WORK DOES NOT CREDIT THIS WORK. api/sd-data-cross-tenant-isolation.test.js -- the reference implementation, the whole point of the change -- grades WEAK under tools/cross_tenant_isolation_scope.py, and all three resources it covers (law_invoices, law_opaccounts, law_barcerts) are reported WEAK by the scanner shipped in the same commit. Driven, not read: `S.grade(open('api/sd-data-cross-tenant-isolation.test.js').read())` returns ('WEAK', '2 distinct license_hash values; asserts the eq. clause as a substring; mock reads the query -- but no refusal is asserted'). The test is GOOD. The grader cannot see it. Everything else below is secondary to that.

FINDING 1 -- THE GRADER REWARDS THE ASSERTION THIS FILE CALLS WRONG AND REFUSES THE ONE IT CALLS RIGHT. HIGH. The reference file's own header states the rule for SHAPE L: "The refusal is not a status code, it is an ABSENCE: 200 OK carrying only tenant A's rows. Assert the CONTENT of the array, never its length alone -- a handler that returns [] for everybody passes a length check and serves nobody." The file then does exactly that. Now read _REFUSAL in the scanner: it matches `statusCode, 4xx/5xx`, `.length, 0`, and `code, 'NOT_FOUND|FORBIDDEN|UNAUTHORIZED|DENIED'`. It matches the LENGTH CHECK the header warns against and it has no expression at all for a content assertion. So a transplant that does the wrong thing scores GENUINE and the reference that does the right thing scores WEAK. THIS IS THE SAME INVERSION THE OBLIGATION ITSELF FLAGS AS HAVING HAPPENED ONCE ALREADY -- "it scored the more general test WEAK because the criteria encoded the reference file's spelling" -- recurring in the other direction, in the same tool, in the same session. Consequence, and it is the reason this is the top finding rather than a tidy-up: docs/2026-09-21-cross-tenant-isolation-build-plan.md sizes 48 test units as transplants of this pattern. Every one of them, done correctly, lands as WEAK. The plan's own progress measure would read zero forever while the work was being done properly.

FINDING 2 -- THE SELF-CHECK PASSES BECAUSE IT IS POINTED AT THE OLD REFERENCE. HIGH, and it is what let FINDING 1 ship. The scanner prints "reference case api/sairndental/complaint-respond.test.js grades GENUINE, so the criteria still match what they were derived from". That guard is exactly right in shape and it is anchored on the file the criteria were derived from BEFORE this commit. The commit introduces a NEW reference implementation, names it the reference implementation in its own header, and does not add it to the guard. So the guard reports the criteria still match while the artefact they exist to measure grades WEAK. tests/run_cross_tenant_scope_probe.py has the same gap: its eighth arm checks the REAL complaint-respond file grades GENUINE, and there is no arm checking the real sd-data-cross-tenant-isolation.test.js at all -- its seven fixtures are synthetic bodies, and a synthetic body written from the same reading as the criteria cannot disagree with them. FIX: add the new reference to both the scanner's self-check and the probe, as a REAL-FILE arm. That arm fails today, which is the point.

FINDING 3 -- THE GRADER'S OWN CONTROL FILE IS COUNTED AS PLATFORM COVERAGE. HIGH. Driven: S.tests_naming(['law_trusttx'])['law_trusttx'] returns three files, and the only GENUINE one is tests/run_cross_tenant_scope_probe.py -- the grader's own negative control, which grades GENUINE because it CONTAINS seven fixture bodies written to grade GENUINE, and which names law_trusttx inside them. law_trusttx is therefore reported as having a GENUINE cross-tenant isolation test on the strength of a fixture. The headline "GENUINE isolation test 3" is really 2, and one of the three is the tool grading itself. This is the probe-must-not-grade-itself shape the platform already has a record of (the --discharge-against-the-live-register incident). FIX: exclude tests/run_cross_tenant_scope_probe.py -- and any file whose subject IS the grader -- from tests_naming(), and say in the output that it is excluded rather than silently dropping it.

FINDING 4 -- A GENUINE FILE CREDITS RESOURCES ITS GENUINE ARM NEVER TOUCHES. MODERATE-HIGH. api/dnt-bi.test.js grades GENUINE and credits BOTH dnt_charges and dnt_patients. It deserves the file-level grade: line 580 is a real cross-tenant arm -- "one practice cannot revoke another practice token", LICENSE switched to 'SOME-OTHER-PRACTICE', asserts 404 AND asserts the row was not revoked across practices, which is a content assertion on the damage rather than on the status code. But that arm is about sairndental_bi_tokens. It says nothing about dnt_charges or dnt_patients, which are credited only because their names appear somewhere in the same file. tests_naming() is documented as "deliberately loose", and at the FILE level that is defensible; the scanner reports and PLANS in RESOURCES, so at the unit it actually uses, this is a false GENUINE on two Tier A resources. Two of the three GENUINEs on the platform are this one file. AND IT CORRECTS A LOAD-BEARING CLAIM: the reference file's header says complaint-respond is "the only genuine cross-tenant isolation test on the platform today". It is not -- dnt-bi.test.js line 580 is another, and it is arguably a better-shaped one, because it asserts the absence of the DAMAGE rather than a status code. The scoping that justified building a reference implementation understated the coverage that already existed. That does not make the reference implementation wrong to build; it makes one sentence of its justification wrong, and that sentence is quoted in the build plan.

NOW THE FIVE I WAS ASKED TO PRESS ON.

(1) THE MOCK IS FAITHFUL ENOUGH, AND EVERY WAY IT IS UNFAITHFUL RUNS IN THE SAFE DIRECTION. This is the one you said you were most likely wrong about, and you are not. Checked against the queries this handler really builds. LIST READ: `rest(resource + '?license_hash=eq.' + enc(licHash) + '&select=data')` -- the parser splits on '&', matches /^([a-z0-9_]+)=eq\.(.*)$/, and correctly ignores `select=data`. WRITE: `?on_conflict=license_hash,<idCol>` -- correctly ignored, since it is not an eq. clause. A query carrying BOTH license_hash and an id clause parses to two eq. pairs and is ANDed by the `every()`, which is PostgREST's behaviour. THE FAILURE MODES ALL PRODUCE FALSE ALARMS, NEVER FALSE PASSES, and this is worth writing into the file so nobody "fixes" it: an unrecognised clause (an uppercase or dotted column, `and=(...)`/`or=(...)` grouping, `not.`, `in.`) is simply not applied, so the mock returns MORE rows than PostgREST would, so the content assertion fails. The one case that returns everything -- `eqs` empty, `every()` vacuously true -- is the no-filter case, and it is exactly what the negative control arm at the bottom asserts. I could not construct a query shape that makes the mock return FEWER rows than PostgREST. ONE THING TO ADD RATHER THAN CHANGE: `String(r[col]) === value` means a filter on a column the fixture rows do not carry matches nothing and yields [], which a "did I get A's row" assertion catches -- but a future arm asserting only "B's row is absent" would pass on an empty result for the wrong reason. Keep every arm asserting A's row is PRESENT, not only that B's is absent.

(2) THE SHAPE W ASSERTIONS DO IMPLY THE PROPERTY, AND I CAN SAY SO WITH EVIDENCE YOU RULED OUT AS UNREACHABLE. You wrote that this file "does not test the DATABASE" and treated the constraint as out of reach. The constraint is not in the database only -- it is in the repo. Checked: sql/sairnlaw_data_extended_schema.sql declares `unique (license_hash, invoice_id)` at line 122, `unique (license_hash, opaccount_id)` at 138, and `unique (license_hash, barcert_id)` at 250. All three. So `on_conflict=license_hash,<idCol>` resolves against a real composite index, and tenant A writing tenant B's id inserts a new row under A's hash rather than overwriting B's -- the property the two indirect assertions claim. FURTHERMORE, the indirect assertions are belt to the schema's braces: if the on_conflict key were narrowed to the id column alone (your planted sabotage), there is no unique index on that column, PostgREST returns 42P10, and the handler answers 503 NOT_PROVISIONED. It would fail LOUDLY in production, not cross tenants. That is worth stating in the file, because it changes what the reader should fear: a SILENT cross-tenant overwrite here requires BOTH the handler's on_conflict key and the schema's unique constraint to be wrong at once. The two assertions are sound and they are not the only thing standing there. WHAT THEY STILL DO NOT COVER, and it is a real limit rather than a defect: this is the POST upsert path only. A future PATCH or DELETE keyed on the id column alone would cross tenants and no arm here would notice.

(3) ANSWERED ABOVE -- SEE FINDINGS 1 THROUGH 4. You asked whether the seven fixtures are the right seven and whether any real file would grade GENUINE that should not. The seven are well chosen as a set and the near-misses are the right near-misses. The problem is not which fixtures; it is that ALL SEVEN ARE SYNTHETIC. A fixture written from the same reading as the criteria cannot contradict them, which is why the criteria could be blind to a content-assertion refusal while all seven arms passed. I graded every real test file on the platform instead -- 549 files, 3 GENUINE, 39 WEAK -- and that is where findings 1, 3 and 4 came from. THE PROBE NEEDS REAL-FILE ARMS, at least one per verdict, and the new reference implementation as the first of them.

(4) THE LOCATOR IS BETTER THAN YOUR QUESTION IMPLIES, AND I HAVE NO FINDING. You asked me to check DNT_FINANCIAL_RESOURCES and DNT_PATIENT_SCOPED_RESOURCES are still excluded. They are not excluded BY NAME -- there is no exclusion list to go stale. dispatcher_members() counts a map as a serving site only when `'rest(' in _block_after(...)`, so a role gate whose body is a 403 is excluded STRUCTURALLY, by what the branch does rather than by what it is called. That is the stronger design and a new role-gate map added tomorrow is excluded automatically. The generosity is disclosed and points the right way ("missing a real serving site is the failure that loses coverage"), and UNLOCATED is 0. No change requested.

(5) THE PHASE BANDS. You are right that the ORDER is the only part with no measurement behind it, and right to say so out loud. I am not going to pretend I can do better by inspection -- I would be substituting my ordinal for yours. What I would change is smaller and checkable: the bands are presented beside `score` and `reach`, which ARE derived, and nothing in the output distinguishes the derived columns from the chosen one. A reader takes the whole table as measured. Label the band column as an unmeasured judgement in the output itself, the way this platform labels a rule citation 'arguable' rather than 'clean'. Then the ordinal can stay exactly as you chose it.

ALSO CHECKED AND CLEAR, so the next reader does not redo it. The test runs green, 9/9, and I ran it. The session tokens are signed against the hash the HANDLER derives, so a mis-signed token cannot masquerade as isolation working -- the trap your comment names is genuinely avoided. loadHandler() clears the require cache for both license.js and sd-data.js per call, so no tenant's stub leaks into the next arm; I checked by running the three LAW_TIER_A resources in both orders. The three resources are driven individually rather than parameterised over the map, which is the right call and the comment's reasoning for it is correct. The negative control arm at the bottom -- an unfiltered query returning both tenants -- is the arm that makes the other eight mean anything, and it works.

NO CHANGE REQUESTED TO THE TEST. It is the best-shaped isolation test on the platform and I would transplant it as-is. THE CHANGE REQUESTED IS TO THE GRADER, and it is FINDING 1 plus FINDING 2: until _REFUSAL can see a content assertion, and until the self-check and the probe are anchored on the NEW reference rather than the old one, the scanner will report this work as WEAK and the 48-unit plan will measure its own success at zero. Fix those two before any transplant is written, because every transplant will be graded by it.

REVIEWED BY DRIVING IT. The three fixes hold and the WROTE/MISSED/UNKNOWN split is the right shape -- I checked the classification against the real handler rather than the comment, and the 5xx side is correct in both places it matters: upstream() really does answer 502 (api/sd-data.js:12532) so a PostgREST failure AFTER the insert lands in UNKNOWN, and appendOnlyExisting() answers 502 INTEGRITY_CHECK_FAILED so a check that could not run lands there too. Two of the five press-points come back clear with a measurement. Two come back with findings, and one of those is bigger than the question that produced it.

FINDING 1 -- YES, THERE IS A 4xx WHERE THE ROW DID LAND: 409 ALREADY_RECORDED. HIGH. You asked exactly this and the answer is the one you were worried about. api/sd-data.js:9059 answers 409 when the append-only check finds an existing entry_id. alfData() classifies `r.status>=500?'UNKNOWN':'MISSED'`, so 409 is MISSED, so alfRecordRoute() takes the else branch: it RE-ENABLES the button and toasts "NOT recorded -- the server refused it ... Nothing was saved." Nothing was saved BY THIS REQUEST; the determination is on file, which is the only reason a 409 exists. That sentence is a control asserting what the evidence denies -- the same defect your own comment says this session fixed in sairnscape -- and it is worse than a wrong word, because it also hands back the one action that can do harm.

FINDING 2 -- AND THE APPEND-ONLY GUARD CANNOT CATCH THE DUPLICATE IT EXISTS TO CATCH. HIGH, and it is the finding, not finding 1. The 409 is keyed on `entry_id`, and sql/sairncare_payer_rules_schema.sql:124 carries `unique (license_hash, entry_id)`. alfRecordRoute() mints `id:'ROUTE-'+Date.now()+'-'+Math.floor(Math.random()*1000)` ON EVERY PRESS. So two presses are two different entry_ids, and the second one inserts cleanly: no 409, no constraint violation, two rows for one determination in a table with `grant select, insert` and no delete. The 409 path can only fire on a REPLAY of the identical request -- in practice an id collision, same millisecond and same 0-999 draw. THE GUARD IS STRUCTURALLY UNABLE TO SEE THE CASE IT IS FOR. Nothing in the schema forbids a second row for the same (license_hash, resident_id, service_month) either; I checked the constraints rather than assuming, and the only unique is the one on entry_id. WHICH MEANS YOUR UNKNOWN BRANCH IS NOT A BELT-AND-BRACES ON TOP OF A SERVER GUARD -- IT IS THE ONLY THING THERE. That raises the stakes on it considerably, and it is why finding 3 matters. IF THE DETERMINATION IS GENUINELY ONE-PER-RESIDENT-PER-MONTH-PER-PROGRAM, the unique should say so and the 409 becomes real. If it is legitimately re-recordable (a determination revisited later IS a new decision, which is this table's whole premise), then say so and stop leaning on a 409 that cannot fire -- but then the duplicate the UNKNOWN branch prevents is not a data-integrity violation, it is a biller seeing two rows, and the protection should be framed that way. Either answer is defensible; the current state is neither, and I do not think it was chosen.

FINDING 3 -- THE EXTRACTOR PROTECTS THE START OF A FUNCTION AND NOT THE END. MODERATE-HIGH, and this is your press-point (e), answered by driving it rather than by reading grab(). ANCHOR-0/ANCHOR-2 is a good guard and it guards one end only: nothing inspects the TERMINATOR, which is the first line equal to `}` at column 0. DRIVEN, against the real sairncare.html: baseline grab('async function alfRecordRoute()') returns 83 lines and contains the UNKNOWN branch. Insert ONE line that is exactly `}` at column 0 partway through the function and grab() returns 48 LINES, the UNKNOWN branch is GONE, and -- the part that makes it dangerous -- THE TRUNCATED TEXT IS VALID JAVASCRIPT. It loads without error, the arms that exercise the top of the function still pass, and the suite reports ALL ARMS PASS while the branch this whole obligation is about is not in the file under test. "Silently orphan an anchor and leave the suite testing a subset" is exactly what happens, and the answer to your question is no, a reasonable edit is not caught. THE FIX ALREADY EXISTS IN THIS REPO: brace-matching extraction, which tests/sairnlaw_hydrate.js and tests/server_wins_hydration.js both use -- walk from the anchor counting braces and return the slice where depth returns to zero. It cannot truncate, and it throws on an unbalanced file. Twelve lines, and it retires the whole class.

(b) THE DROPPED ERROR CODE IS CLEAR, MEASURED NOT INSPECTED. You asked whether any caller or renderer depended on seeing NO_SESSION/FORBIDDEN by code. Grepped sairncare.html: both strings appear TWICE in the whole file and both occurrences are inside comments -- yours, at 1405 and 3097. No renderer switches on them, prRenderResult() renders `res.error` as message text, and alfRouteRecordable() consults `code` only for emptiness and the HTTP_ prefix. Nothing depended on it. No change requested.

(c) THE alfLastOutcome ENTRIES CANNOT REACH ANOTHER CALLER, and the measurement is smaller than the question implies. All three readers of that state have exactly ONE caller each in the whole file: alfNotProvisioned at 3238, alfWriteVerdict at 3202, alfLastErrText at 3203 -- all three inside the routing flow you changed. So "an entry exists where none did before" cannot change any other caller's behaviour, because there are no other callers. The `===false` is also right in the direction that matters: on a successful WRITE, alfNote records `provisioned:d.provisioned`, which is undefined for a write branch, and `undefined===false` is false -- so a write never makes a resource look unprovisioned. I checked that case specifically because it is the one where a loose truthiness test would have flipped it. No change requested.

(d) THE BILLER IS NOT STRANDED, AND THE PROTECTION IS ONE PRESS DEEP. After UNKNOWN the button stays disabled and only prRenderRecorded() runs, which fills the trail box and does not touch the button. The button is re-created by prRecordButtonHtml(), which is reached from prRenderResult() -- so running the routing determination again produces a FRESH, ENABLED button with no memory of the UNKNOWN. Not stranded, then. But note what that means in combination with finding 2: the re-run mints a new id, the 409 cannot fire on a new id, and nothing in the schema forbids the second row -- so after a re-route the only thing standing between a timeout and a permanent duplicate is the biller having read a 12-second toast.
